description: Excalidraw's 39-second launch video for the Excalidraw CLI, which renders Excalidraw diagrams from Excalidraw+ or local files so AI agents can see and check their own diagrams. The video pairs a hand-drawn title ('Render any scene to PNG') with a clean terminal session listing and rendering scenes. It's a strong reference for a short, focused developer-tool intro: one capability, shown in the product's own visual language, ending on a one-line call to action ('Install today').
text:
Excalidraw CLI released!

Log in to your Excalidraw+ account or use with local files.

You can easily render Excalidraw diagrams to give better output feedback to your agents.

Install today.
replies_summary: Overwhelmingly positive and practical: most replies latch onto the agent 'render loop' — letting agents render and look at their own diagrams so humans can spot misunderstandings fast — and several users report already adding it to workflows. Recurring questions are about pricing ('Is it free to use?'), CLI vs. MCP, and whether the rendered PNG flows back into the agent's context; a few push long-standing feature requests (subfolders) or name alternatives (tldraw, Mermaid). Quote posts echo the same theme ('My agents will love this') across English, Japanese, Turkish, Portuguese, Chinese and Korean audiences.

notable_replies.text: A CLI for diagrams is sneaky useful: agents can render what they think the system looks like, and humans can spot the misunderstanding in seconds.
letting agents render and look at their own output is so underrated.
Tried it. Great work, adding it to my daily workflows.
But what about a simple feature like subfolders? It’s been pending for years 😅

https://t.co/zbcYD8xQKf

One jokes about spending 20 years removing buttons only to buy keypads again; the rest of the thread is account-suspension complaints unrelated to the post.

notable_replies.text: Mapping a repeated prompt to a physical key is a smart touch. So much agent work right now is typing the same "run the tests and fix what fails" line again and again.
we spent 20 years removing buttons from everything and now we're buying keypads to talk to the AI. progress

description: Emil Kowalski on a motion-design principle for UI: bigger elements (and longer distances) should animate more slowly because they feel heavier, illustrated with a hand vs. cursors animation. Reference for animation timing on websites and interfaces.
text:
The bigger an animated element is, the slower it should move.

Notice how the hand on the right moves much slower than the cursors on the left. That’s because it feels heavier.

The same applies to distance. The more an element has to travel, the longer the animation should be. https://t.co/lFDygrDF4u
replies_summary: Strong agreement that matching mass/distance to duration is what makes motion 'feel right'. Commenters extend it to static spacing and ask whether to scale duration linearly; motion-school folks note it's a classic principle.

notable_replies.text: Works for static layouts too. The bigger the element, the more room it needs around it.  Same physics, just frozen.
this is the kind of detail that separates "works" from "feels right".

description: Warp introduces Warp Factories, 'Terraform for agents': one repository that configures agents, automations, access/environments and measurement as code. A very high-reach (~955K impressions) reference for explaining an abstract platform concept with an analogy plus a demo video.
text:
Agents are getting complex to manage: models, skills, automations, permissions, cloud environments, orchestration patterns...

So, we built the Terraform for agents: one repository that configures all of your agents as code.

The Warp Factories configuration spec defines:
- Agents and orchestration: how work gets routed and which models agents use
- Automations: the events and schedules that kick off work
- Access and environments: repositories, secrets, MCP servers, and runners
- Measurement: scorers and benchmarks for understanding and improving performance

Because it’s all code, both engineers and agents can propose changes to the factory itself. That makes it possible to test new configurations, benchmark them, and even have your factory propose improvements as PRs.
replies_summary: Engaged and mostly constructive: replies agree that managing agents is becoming its own discipline and that agents-as-code is the right shape. They raise version pinning, permissions and revoke paths, with some irony about writing YAML to manage AI.

notable_replies.text: we've come full circle: AI was supposed to delete YAML. now we're writing YAML to manage the AI.
